where: Exam traps, trap 1 (also Section 1 first paragraph and worked example step 2)
problem: The chapter uses the word 'length' for two different things and the trap states the wrong one. It says a one-hot vector's length is |V|, but the Euclidean length (norm) of a one-hot vector is 1, which worked example step 2 correctly computes and the formula box uses (|a| = √(a·a)). |V| is the dimension, i.e. the number of entries. As written, the trap directly contradicts the worked example and the cosine formula, and a student cannot tell which value to substitute for |a| and |b|.
fix: Use 'dimension' for the number of entries and 'length' or 'norm' only for |a|. Trap 1 becomes: 'A one-hot vector's dimension is |V|, the vocabulary size, so all words use the same number of entries. Its Euclidean length is always 1, because exactly one entry equals 1.' Rewrite Section 1 as: 'The one-hot vector e_w has dimension |V| and Euclidean length 1.'

problem: 'The dense geometry can place cricket near bat and far from ball' is a bad illustration: cricket and ball are strongly related and co-occur constantly, so trained dense vectors put them close, not far apart. The example teaches the opposite of how distributional vectors behave.
fix: Use a genuinely unrelated word: 'can place cricket near bat and far from monsoon, even when the words never share a sentence'.

problem: It says to state whether you use U or UΣ 'before comparing by cosine'. Row w of U_k Σ_k is just row w of U_k multiplied by one scalar (its singular value), and cosine is invariant to per-vector scaling, so the choice cannot change any cosine. It only changes dot products and Euclidean distances.
fix: 'SVD gives U, Σ and Vᵀ, and row w of U_kΣ_k is row w of U_k scaled by σ_w. Cosine is unaffected by that scaling, but dot products and Euclidean distances are not; state which you use before using either.'

problem: 'This use of SVD on word-context counts is latent semantic analysis (LSA)' does not match the standard definition: in most textbooks LSA is SVD applied to a term-document matrix (often weighted by tf-idf or log-entropy), and SVD on a word-word PPMI matrix is usually described as a count-based distributional embedding.
fix: 'This use of SVD on a word-context count matrix is a count-based distributional method; the same idea applied to a term-document matrix is latent semantic analysis (LSA).'

problem: The one-hot rows have three cells while the dense rows have two, in a table whose title names only two dense columns. Two different vector spaces of different dimension are shown in one grid, so a student may read 0.8 as an entry in dimension 1 of a three-dimensional space, or think the dense vectors lost an entry.
fix: Show the dense vectors in their own two-column table (dim1, dim2) labelled 'dense vectors, dimension 2 (independent of |V| = 3)', and keep the three-column table for the one-hot vectors only.
